course.title: UX and Human–Computer Interaction
course.description: How people see, remember and decide at a screen, and how to find out whether a design works for them. Covers research methods, usability heuristics, interaction design and accessibility to WCAG 2.2.
course.audience: A capable adult who uses software every day and has never studied why some interfaces work and others fail. They know basic proportions and percentages and have met the idea of a sample. No design or coding experience is needed; two lessons read short HTML snippets.

paragraphs: A screen is read in two stages. In the first, which lasts a fraction of a second, the eye groups elements by their distances, colours and edges before it takes in any word, and in the second the words are read within the groups that the first stage made. This course begins with that first stage and with the limits of memory and movement that every layout has to respect, using two formulas, Fitts's law for pointing and Hick's law for choosing, to turn those limits into numbers.

Knowing how people see and act does not tell you what a particular group of people needs, so the middle of the course covers how to find out. You will see when to interview and when to survey, how a card sort and a tree test show whether content is where people expect it, how many users a usability test needs, and how to tell a real difference in an A/B test from chance. Each method comes with the arithmetic that shows what it can and cannot support.

The last two modules turn findings into judgements and into requirements. Nielsen's ten heuristics and a severity scale let you inspect an interface and decide what to fix first, and the lessons on forms and on WCAG 2.2 cover error messages, colour contrast, keyboard operation, text alternatives and target size, each with a check you can run on a real page.
outcomes: You'll be able to explain why a screen is read the way it is, using grouping, attention and memory limits.
You'll be able to calculate pointing difficulty with Fitts's law and choice time with Hick's law, and say what each does not tell you.
You'll be able to choose a research method (interview, survey, card sort, usability test, A/B test) for a given question, and spot a leading question.
You'll be able to judge an interface against Nielsen's ten heuristics and rate the severity of what you find.
You'll be able to check a colour pair, a touch target and a form against the relevant WCAG 2.2 success criteria.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Psychology: How Minds Work, Probability and Statistics.

modules.title: How people see, remember and act
modules.description: The limits of perception, memory and movement that every layout works within.

modules.title: Finding out what users need
modules.description: Interviews, surveys, card sorts, usability tests and experiments, and what each can and cannot show.

modules.title: Judging and shaping interactions
modules.description: Heuristics, expert inspection, severity, and the details of forms, errors and feedback.

modules.title: Accessibility
modules.description: WCAG 2.2 as a working checklist: contrast, keyboard, structure and target size.

concepts.title: Gestalt grouping
concepts.summary: Viewers perceive nearby, similar, enclosed or aligned elements as belonging together before they read any of them.

concepts.title: Visual hierarchy
concepts.summary: Size, contrast and position set the order in which a viewer's attention visits elements on a screen.

concepts.title: Working memory
concepts.summary: The small store that holds the items a person is using right now, estimated at roughly four chunks in recent work.

concepts.title: Chunking
concepts.summary: Grouping items into meaningful units so that more information fits in the same number of slots.

concepts.title: Recognition versus recall
concepts.summary: Picking an item from a visible set takes less memory than producing it from nothing.

concepts.title: Fitts's law
concepts.summary: Time to reach a target grows with the index of difficulty ID = log2(D/W + 1), where D is distance to the target and W its width along the line of motion (Shannon formulation).

concepts.title: Hick's law
concepts.summary: For n equally likely choices the decision time grows as b·log2(n + 1).

concepts.title: Response-time limits
concepts.summary: About 0.1 s feels instant, 1 s keeps the flow of thought, and 10 s is the limit of attention on a task.

concepts.title: Mental model
concepts.summary: A person's working picture of how a system behaves, which may differ from how it is built.

concepts.title: Signifier
concepts.summary: A perceivable cue that shows where and how an action can be taken.

concepts.title: Gulf of execution
concepts.summary: The gap between what a user wants to do and the actions the system makes available and visible.

concepts.title: Gulf of evaluation
concepts.summary: The gap between the system's state and the user's ability to perceive and interpret it.

concepts.title: Leading question
concepts.summary: A question whose wording suggests the answer wanted.

concepts.title: Margin of error
concepts.summary: For a proportion p from n independent responses, 95% margin = 1.96·sqrt(p(1−p)/n).

concepts.title: Say versus do
concepts.summary: What people report about their behaviour often differs from what they do.

concepts.title: Card sort
concepts.summary: Participants group content items into categories, showing the structure they expect.

concepts.title: Tree test
concepts.summary: Participants find items in a text-only hierarchy, measuring whether the structure and labels work.

concepts.title: Breadth and depth
concepts.summary: A hierarchy with b choices per level and d levels can reach b^d items.

concepts.title: Think-aloud protocol
concepts.summary: Participants speak their thoughts while they work on a task, revealing what they notice and expect.

concepts.title: Problem discovery model
concepts.summary: With a per-user detection rate L, n users find a proportion 1 − (1 − L)^n of the problems; Nielsen and Landauer's average L was about 0.31.

concepts.title: System Usability Scale
concepts.summary: Ten five-point items scored (odd items: response − 1; even items: 5 − response), summed and multiplied by 2.5, range 0 to 100.

concepts.title: A/B test
concepts.summary: Randomly assign users to two versions and compare a metric.

concepts.title: Two-proportion z
concepts.summary: z = (p2 − p1) / sqrt(p1(1−p1)/n1 + p2(1−p2)/n2); at the 95% level |z| must exceed 1.96.

concepts.title: The why gap
concepts.summary: Analytics show what users did, and give no reason.

concepts.title: Usability heuristic
concepts.summary: A broad rule of thumb for judging an interface, derived from patterns in found problems.

concepts.title: Nielsen's ten heuristics
concepts.summary: Visibility of system status; match between system and real world; user control and freedom; consistency and standards; error prevention; recognition rather than recall; flexibility and efficiency of use; aesthetic and minimalist design; help users recognise, diagnose and recover from errors; help and documentation.

concepts.title: Heuristic evaluation
concepts.summary: Several evaluators independently inspect an interface against heuristics and then merge their findings.

concepts.title: Severity rating
concepts.summary: A 0–4 scale, from not a problem to usability catastrophe, based on frequency, impact and persistence.

concepts.title: Cognitive walkthrough
concepts.summary: An evaluator steps through a task asking, at each action, whether the user will try it, notice it, connect it to the goal and see progress.

concepts.title: Error prevention
concepts.summary: Design that makes the error impossible or unlikely, such as constraints, defaults and reversible actions.

concepts.title: Anatomy of an error message
concepts.summary: A good error message says what happened, why, and what to do next, in the user's words, next to the field.

concepts.title: Undo over confirmation
concepts.summary: Allowing a reversal is usually better than asking 'Are you sure?', which users answer by habit.

concepts.title: POUR
concepts.summary: WCAG organises requirements under four principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.

concepts.title: Conformance levels
concepts.summary: Success criteria are levelled A, AA and AAA; AA is the usual legal and policy target.

concepts.title: Contrast ratio
concepts.summary: (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the lighter colour's relative luminance; AA needs 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and for key interface components (1.4.3, 1.4.11).

concepts.title: Keyboard operability
concepts.summary: Every function works from a keyboard (2.1.1), focus is visible (2.4.7) and not hidden behind other content (2.4.11).

concepts.title: Semantic markup
concepts.summary: Native elements such as button, label, and headings give assistive technology a name, role and state without extra code (4.1.2).

concepts.title: Target size minimum
concepts.summary: Pointer targets must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or have enough spacing (2.5.8, AA, new in WCAG 2.2).

lessons.title: How the eye groups a screen

lead.text: Six dots stand in a row. The gaps between neighbouring dots, from left to right, are 8 px, 40 px, 8 px, 40 px and 8 px, and the dots are identical in colour, size and shape. Decide how many groups a viewer will see before reading on.

reveal.text: Three groups of two: the 8 px gaps join dots and the 40 px gaps separate the pairs. The next screen names the rule.

steps.headline: Elements that sit closer to each other than to their neighbours are read as a group.

lead.text: The figure shows the same six dots twice. In the first view they are evenly spaced and the eye sees a single row, and in the second the gaps alternate between 8 px and 40 px and the same dots become three pairs. Nothing but distance has changed. Grouping by nearness is called **proximity**, and it is a comparison between gaps, so the 8 px that joins two dots in one layout would separate them in another where every gap was 2 px.

afterFigure.text: Max Wertheimer described grouping by proximity, and by the similarity treated on the next screen, in a paper of 1923, as part of the Gestalt school of psychology, which holds that a viewer perceives organised wholes before the parts that make them up. The consequence for a form is the one in the opening figure: a label must be nearer to its own field than to any other element, so that the gap, which is seen first, agrees with the words, which are read second.

steps.headline: Shared appearance and a shared enclosure each join elements, and either can outweigh a gap.

lead.text: Proximity is one cue among several. In the figure every dot is the same distance from its neighbours, so distance says nothing, yet each view still shows three pairs. In the first the pairs share a colour, in the second a shape, and in the third each pair sits inside a rounded box. Elements that look alike are read as members of one set, a cue called **similarity**, and elements that sit inside one outline or on one background panel are read as a single unit, a cue called **common region**.

afterFigure.text: Common region is the strongest of the three, because an outline is an explicit boundary, and it can override proximity: two buttons 8 px apart in separate panels read as separate, while two buttons 40 px apart on one panel read as together. It is also why a pale panel behind a set of related controls works without any border line. Similarity needs more care, because it asserts likeness: a viewer who sees two things in the same colour takes them to be alike in function, and the last screens return to that.

lead.text: Apply the cues to a settings page. Every control on it is 24 px from its neighbours, and a pale panel is placed behind just three related controls: font size, line spacing and theme.

reveal.text: The panel is an outline in everything but name. It groups the three controls although the gaps around them are the same as everywhere else.

steps.headline: Elements that share an edge read as a column, and a line of items reads as a row.

lead.text: Two further cues act along lines. Elements whose left edges fall on the same vertical line are read as a **column**, and the eye follows that edge down the page, which is why a ragged left edge makes a list look as though it has no structure. The second view of the figure draws the same five bars in the same rows, and the shared edge alone groups them. A row of icons at one height with one spacing is read as a row for a related reason: the eye tends to carry on in the direction it is already moving, a cue called **continuity**, and an element that leaves the line is read as a break in the sequence.

afterFigure.text: Alignment is the cheapest grouping cue, because it costs no extra space or ink, and designers use it for most of a page and keep boxes and colours for the few places that need a stronger cue. It also explains why a divider line is rarely needed: when two groups are separated by a wider gap, the gap already separates them, and a rule drawn through it adds a second mark for the eye to process.

steps.headline: Diagnose the sign-up form and repair it using gaps alone.

workedSteps.text: Measure the two gaps around the label Password: it is 8 px below the Email field and 24 px above the Password field.
Proximity compares the gaps and the smaller one wins, so the label joins the Email field, which is the wrong one.
Work out how many px nearer the label is to the wrong field than to its own.
Swap the two gaps so that the label sits 4 px above its own field and 24 px below the previous field. It is then 20 px nearer the field it names, and no new element has been added.

steps.headline: Attention visits large, high-contrast and well-placed elements first, and a squint shows the order.

lead.text: Grouping decides what belongs together; **visual hierarchy** decides what is looked at first. Three properties set it: the size of an element, its contrast with the background, and its position, since in languages read from left to right the eye starts at the top left of a page. In the first view of the figure the heading is the largest and darkest text and the button is the only filled shape, so those two are visited before the body text and the small caption.

A quick test is to squint at a page, or blur it, until the words can no longer be read. What remains is the pattern of dark and coloured masses, and the second view shows that pattern for the sale page: the heading and the button survive and the body text fades into grey, which is the order in which a viewer will visit them.

afterFigure.text: A hierarchy should match the importance of the content, and the squint is a way of checking that it does. If the button the page exists for disappears when you squint, or a decorative banner is the darkest thing in the blur, the page is ranking the wrong things first.

lead.text: Look back at the squinted page. It ranked the heading first, the button second and the body text last, according to size, contrast and position.

reveal.text: That ranking is the page's visual hierarchy. It can be changed without moving anything, by making an element larger, darker or more different from its surroundings.

steps.headline: Colour and shape assert likeness, so reusing one for unrelated things misleads.

lead.text: When two cues give different groupings, the viewer hesitates. In the figure the gaps make three pairs, but in the second view colour joins dots across the wide gaps, and the eye cannot settle on either reading. The same happens with a reused style. On a page where links are blue and underlined, the viewer learns after a few examples that blue underline means a link, and a phrase of ordinary text that is styled the same way is then clicked, and found to do nothing.

afterFigure.text: Colour is therefore part of the meaning of a page and not decoration. Each time a colour or a shape is used, it tells the viewer that this element belongs with the others that wear it, so a style should be reserved for the one kind of thing it names. When a grouping looks wrong, the cause is usually two cues pulling against each other, and the repair is to change the weaker one so that they agree.

lead.text: Four buttons stand in a row with equal gaps of 8 px between neighbours. A panel is then drawn around the first two buttons and another panel around the last two. Say how many groups the viewer sees now.

reveal.text: Two groups: with equal gaps alone the row would be read as one, but a shared region is an explicit boundary and outweighs distance.

lessons.orientation: How proximity, similarity, common region and alignment decide which elements a viewer reads as one group, and how hierarchy orders them.
lessons.reviewLabel: How the eye groups a screen
lessons.nextAction: Count how many items working memory can hold, and design so that people need to remember fewer.

blocks.text: In a sign-up form the label Password sits 8 px below the Email field and 24 px above the Password field it names. No one has read a word yet, and already the eye has attached the label to the Email field above it, because the smaller gap says that two things belong together. The figure shows the form with its distances marked, and its second view moves the label to 4 px above its own field and 24 px below the previous one, which repairs the form without adding a line, a box or a word.

A layout is read twice, first as shapes, in a fraction of a second, and then as words. The first reading decides what the words are taken to mean, so a form that groups wrongly has its text misread even when the text is perfect, and the eye follows rules in making that first reading.

intro.whyItMatters: A wrong grouping causes errors that no amount of clear wording can repair.

recap.keyIdea: Viewers read nearness, shared appearance, shared enclosure and shared edges as grouping before they read any word, and size, contrast and position set the order in which the groups are visited.

blocks.text: You saw that a label nearer to the wrong field is read as belonging to it, and that proximity is a comparison between gaps, so it can be repaired by moving a label alone. Similarity and common region group at any distance, with common region the stronger, and alignment groups at no cost. When two cues disagree the viewer hesitates, so a colour or a shape should be used for one kind of thing only.

lessons.title: What memory can hold

lead.text: A 16-digit card number is shown as four groups of four digits, and a person learns each group as one unit. Decide how many units that person has to hold.

reveal.text: Four units. The next screen gives the name for such a unit and the limit that makes the count matter.

steps.headline: Working memory holds only a few chunks, so grouping lets the same capacity carry more.

lead.text: The store used for the items a person is working with right now is called **working memory**, and its capacity is small. George Miller's paper of 1956, "The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two", is the source of the figure many people quote, but Miller was describing the span for items, and he noted that the unit could be stretched by recoding. Nelson Cowan reviewed the evidence in 2001 and argued that the limit is nearer four. Neither number is a design rule to be applied exactly, and the safe reading is that the store is very small.

What fills it is not the number of digits or words but the number of units. A **chunk** is a group of items that a person already treats as one thing, such as a familiar phone-number group or a well-known word, and **chunking** is the grouping of items into chunks. In the figure the same eleven digits overflow four slots when they are separate, and fit when they are grouped as 077, 009, 001 and 23.

afterFigure.text: Chunking depends on what the reader already knows. To someone who knows the letters, FBI is one chunk, and to someone who does not, it is three, so a designer chunks a string by splitting it where readers expect the splits to fall.

lead.text: Grouping the eleven digits turned them into four units, each of which the reader treats as one thing.

reveal.text: That unit is what the rest of the lesson counts. A screen should be judged by how many chunks it asks a person to carry, not by how many characters it contains.

lead.text: A settings page has a menu of forty options, and users find it hard to locate the one they want. Decide whether this is a memory problem or something else.

reveal.text: The options are all on screen, so nothing has to be remembered. The next screen explains why that matters.

steps.headline: Picking from a visible set takes less memory than producing an answer from nothing.

lead.text: There are two ways of getting an item out of memory. In **recall** the person produces it with no cue on the screen, as when they type a command at a blank prompt, and in **recognition** the person picks it from options that are shown, as when they choose Copy from a menu. Recognition is easier because the options act as cues, and nothing has to be held in working memory until it is needed. Jakob Nielsen's list of usability heuristics states this as a rule: recognition rather than recall.

The same difference separates a password field, where the user must produce the password, from a saved-password prompt, where the browser offers it. A long menu is a search problem, because the cost is scanning, and the memory problem appears only when a user must remember the name of an option that is not on screen.

afterFigure.text: Keep the state of the task on screen, so that the user does not have to remember it. Show the code on the same page where it is needed, keep related choices together, and split long strings into groups, since each of these removes something from working memory.

workedSteps.text: Without grouping, every digit is its own item, so the string asks for eleven items.
Grouped as 077 009 001 23, each group is read as one unit, which gives four chunks.

steps.headline: A screen adds load of its own, and the task has a load that cannot be removed.

lead.text: Every task asks for some memory and attention, and **cognitive load** is the name for the total. Part of it comes from the task itself: an accountant adding a column of figures must hold the running total whatever the screen looks like. Another part is added by the layout, as when two related fields are on different pages or a code must be remembered across a page change, and this part is called **extraneous load**, because the design could remove it.

Design aims at extraneous load, since it can be reduced and the load of the task cannot. A checkout that says "enter the code from the previous page" puts a six-digit code in memory, while one that shows the code beside the box removes it entirely, leaving all of working memory for the order itself.
A checkout shows a six-digit code as two groups of three, then moves to a new page and asks the user to type it.

reveal.text: The user must carry two chunks across the page change. Putting the code on the page where it is typed removes that load, which is the cheapest improvement available.

lead.text: A software installer displays a 20-character licence key in five groups of four and asks the user to type it into another window. Work out how many chunks the user would need to hold.

reveal.text: Five chunks is above the roughly four that working memory holds, so the sensible design is to keep the key visible beside the box, or to let the user copy and paste it.

lessons.orientation: Working memory is small, chunking makes it go further, and recognition spares it altogether.

blocks.text: Try this with the eleven digits 0 7 7 0 0 9 0 0 1 2 3: read them once, look away, and write them down. Most people drop a digit or two. Now read them as 077 009 001 23 and write them down again, and the task becomes much easier, although the digits and their order are the same.

What changed is the number of things you had to hold. Eleven separate digits are eleven items, but the grouped version is four units, and the mind can keep a few units in an active store while it works. The limits of that store are among the most reliable facts in psychology, and a screen that ignores them asks the user to do the one thing people do worst.

recap.keyIdea: Working memory holds only a few chunks, so a screen should group items into chunks and show options and state instead of asking people to remember them.

blocks.text: You counted units and not characters, and found that sixteen digits can cost four chunks while the same digits unbroken cost sixteen. Recognition keeps the options on screen, so it asks for far less than recall, and extraneous load such as a code carried across pages is the part of the load a design can remove.

lessons.title: Distance, size and the number of choices

lead.text: In Fitts's experiments, the time to reach a target depended on the distance to it and on its width. A target is 1 cm wide and 7 cm away. Decide whether halving the distance or doubling the width helps more.

reveal.text: The two changes help by the same amount. The next screen shows why.

steps.headline: Time to reach a target depends on the ratio of its distance to its width.

lead.text: Paul Fitts's tapping experiments of 1954 asked people to move between two targets as fast as they could, and found that movement was quicker for wider and nearer targets, and that speed was traded against accuracy. In human-computer interaction the result is written in the form I. Scott MacKenzie popularised in 1992: the **index of difficulty**, ID = log2(D/W + 1), measured in bits, where D is the distance to the target and W is its width along the line of motion.

The figure shows the opening example. With D = 7 cm and W = 1 cm the ratio is 7, and log2(7 + 1) = log2(8) = 3 bits. Doubling W to 2 cm gives a ratio of 3.5 and an ID of log2(4.5), about 2.17 bits. Because D and W enter only as a ratio, halving the distance would have given the same 3.5, which is why neither change beats the other.

afterFigure.text: The index does not give a time directly. The movement time is modelled as a straight-line function of it, MT = a + b × ID, where a and b are constants found by measuring the particular device and user. The formula therefore ranks designs reliably, and predicts an absolute time only after its constants have been measured.

steps.headline: Work out the index of difficulty for D = 7 cm with W = 1 cm, then with W = 2 cm.

workedSteps.text: The distance is 7 cm and the width is 1 cm, so D/W is 7.
Add 1 and take the base-2 logarithm, since 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
Now widen the target to 2 cm. Work out the new ID, to two decimal places.

lead.text: Use the same steps for a smaller case. The target is 2 cm wide and 6 cm from the pointer.

reveal.text: D/W is 3 and 3 + 1 = 4, a power of 2, which is why the logarithm comes out whole.

steps.headline: A screen edge stops the pointer, so a target there behaves as if it were unlimited in size.

lead.text: The width in Fitts's law is measured along the line of motion, and a mouse pointer cannot travel past the edge of the screen. A button at the top edge, such as the menu bar on many desktops, can therefore be reached by pushing the pointer upward as far as it will go, with no need to stop precisely, and a corner target gains the same advantage in two directions. In the model, the width W of such a target is effectively unlimited, and its index of difficulty falls to a small value.

Three design rules follow. Make the primary button large, since W sits in the denominator. Put controls that are used together near each other, since D falls. Place a destructive button away from the ones used often, since a high ID makes an accidental hit less likely, which is the one case where difficulty is a feature.
Look again at why a button on the top edge of the screen is easier to hit than the same button floating in the middle.

reveal.text: The edge removes the need to stop. In Fitts's terms the target's size along the movement is no longer limited by its drawn height.

steps.headline: Decision time grows with the logarithm of the number of equally likely choices.

lead.text: Choosing has its own law. William Hick in 1952 and Ray Hyman in 1953 found that the time to choose among n equally likely options grows as log2(n + 1), multiplied by a constant b found by measurement. A menu of 7 items gives log2(8) = 3, and a menu of 15 gives log2(16) = 4. Doubling the list therefore adds one unit of b, and does not double the time.

This is why Hick's law is not the same as saying that fewer items are always better. The time grows slowly, so a well-organised list of 15 can beat a menu of three levels, where each level costs its own decision and its own page. The law also assumes that the options are equally likely and that the user does not already know where the item is, and it ignores labels and grouping, which affect real choices a great deal.

steps.headline: Three response times mark how people experience a system: 0.1 s, 1 s and 10 s.

lead.text: A selection that takes a person 3 units to make is useless if the system then takes ten seconds to answer, so the last quantity to know is how long a screen can take. Robert Miller's study of 1968 and later work by Nielsen give three limits. About **0.1 s** feels instant, so that the user sees the response as caused directly by the action. About **1 s** keeps the flow of thought uninterrupted, although the user notices the delay. About **10 s** is the limit of attention on a task, and beyond it people turn to something else.

A response slower than the limit calls for feedback: a pressed state within 0.1 s, a progress indicator for anything slower than a second, and a percentage or a time estimate for delays near ten seconds.
A list of 15 equally likely items grows to 31 items, the same sort of doubling that took the list from 7 to 15. Work out how much the log2(n + 1) term increases.

reveal.text: Each doubling adds one unit. A designer who halves the number of items per screen gains one unit, but adds a level of navigation that costs its own decision.

blocks.text: A target 1 cm wide and 7 cm from the pointer has an index of difficulty of log2(8), which is exactly 3 bits. Widen the target to 2 cm and the index drops to log2(4.5), about 2.17 bits. The numbers describe how long a hand takes to land on a button, and the relationship has held since Paul Fitts measured it in tapping experiments in 1954.

A formula of this kind lets a designer compare two layouts before building either, because the time to reach a target depends on only two measurements. A second formula, from William Hick and Ray Hyman, does the same for the time taken to choose among options, and together they cover most of what happens between seeing a screen and acting on it.

recap.keyIdea: The time to point depends on the ratio of distance to width through ID = log2(D/W + 1), the time to choose grows as log2(n + 1), and neither formula includes familiarity, labels or grouping.

blocks.text: You calculated the index of difficulty for several targets, and saw that edges and corners behave as if they were unlimited in size. For choice, doubling a list adds one unit and not twice the time, which makes organisation a better lever than cutting items. Response-time limits of 0.1 s, 1 s and 10 s then say how long a system may take before the user needs feedback.

steps.headline: A user acts on their own picture of the system, and the screen is the only thing that can shape it.

lead.text: A person's working picture of how a system behaves is their **mental model**, and it is built from experience, guesses and whatever the screen shows. It may differ from how the system is actually built, and still be useful, as when someone treats a thermostat as a tap that makes the room warmer faster the higher it is set. The designer has a model too, the one the system was built to follow, and the two people never meet.

What connects them is the **system image**, which is everything the user can see and do: the labels, the layout, the feedback, the manual. The first view of the figure shows the successful case, in which the image carries the designer's model across so that the user's picture matches the real behaviour. In the second the image says too little, and the user fills the gap with a guess.

afterFigure.text: Because the system image is the only channel, a user whose picture is wrong has usually been given a poor image. The design must therefore show what can be done and what has happened, and the remaining two terms name those two jobs.

steps.headline: An affordance is what an object allows, and a signifier is the cue that shows it.

lead.text: James Gibson coined the word **affordance** in 1979 for what an environment allows an animal to do, and Don Norman brought it into design in 1988. A door affords pushing, and a chair affords sitting, whether or not anyone can tell. The word is often misused for any visible hint on a screen, which is a different thing: a hint that is perceivable and says where and how to act is a **signifier**, a term Norman introduced in the revised edition of The Design of Everyday Things in 2013.

A flat plate on a door is a signifier for pushing, because there is nothing to grip, and a handle is a signifier for pulling. A button's raised edge, a link's underline and a text field's box are signifiers on a screen. A signifier can be missing, as when an affordance exists and nothing shows it, and it can be wrong, as when a handle is fitted to a door that must be pushed.
A raised edge on a button shows that it can be pressed, although the button would work without it.

reveal.text: The raised edge is a signifier. The button's ability to be pressed is the affordance.

steps.headline: Between a goal and an outcome lie two gaps: one in acting, one in reading the result.

lead.text: Norman describes using a system as a loop. The user forms a goal, plans an action and carries it out, the system changes, and the user perceives the new state, interprets it and compares it with the goal. The figure shows the loop with its stages, and a failure can arise at either side of the system box.

The **gulf of execution** is the gap between what the user wants to do and the actions the system makes available and visible. In the second view an icon-only toolbar has no labels, so the user who wants to export cannot tell which action is the right one. The **gulf of evaluation** is the gap between the system's state and the user's ability to perceive and interpret it. In the third view a thermostat shows only the target temperature, so the user has set it correctly and still cannot tell whether the heating is running.

afterFigure.text: Both gulfs are properties of the design, since each depends on what the system shows. When a user fails, the first question is which stage of the loop gave way, and the answer tells the designer where to repair.

lead.text: Apply the loop to a photo editor with a row of icons and no labels, where the user wants to rotate the photo.

reveal.text: The goal is clear and the available action is hidden among similar icons. That is a gap in execution, and a label or tooltip narrows it.

steps.headline: Walk through the loop for a thermostat that displays only the target temperature.

workedSteps.text: The user wants the room to be warmer, which is the goal.
They plan to raise the target and act by turning the dial up, which the thermostat allows and shows clearly.
The display now shows the new target and says nothing about whether the heating is on, so the user cannot interpret what is happening.
Name the gap that this leaves between the system's state and the user's ability to read it.

steps.headline: Constraints, mapping and feedback narrow the two gulfs.

lead.text: A design narrows the gulf of execution by making the available actions visible and by limiting the wrong ones. A **constraint** limits the options, as a plug that fits one way only, and a **mapping** is the relation between a control and its effect, which is natural when the layout of the controls copies the layout of the things they control, as on a stove whose four knobs sit in the same square as its four burners.

It narrows the gulf of evaluation with **feedback**, which is a visible, immediate report of what the system did, such as a button that changes as it is pressed and a message that says what was saved. A system with all three offers a way to act and a way to check, so that the loop closes.
A door can be pushed, whatever its appearance. Use the vocabulary of the lesson to name what the door permits.

reveal.text: A door affords pushing, and the plate or handle is only the signifier that shows or contradicts it.

lead.text: A user fails to find the Export command and says, "I am just not good with computers." A designer using this lesson's terms would look elsewhere for the fault.

reveal.text: Locate the failure in the design and a repair follows, such as a label, a tooltip or a menu item where people look.

lessons.title: Asking people: interviews and surveys

lead.text: A team wants to know whether people can find things with its new search. Decide which of the two wordings in the figure is more likely to give an honest answer.

reveal.text: The question about the last thing they looked for. The next screen gives the reason.

steps.headline: People describe what they did more reliably than what they would want, so ask about the past.

lead.text: The two main ways of asking are the interview and the survey. An **interview** is a conversation with one person at a time, in which the questions are open and the interviewer follows up, and it answers why. A **survey** gives the same closed questions to many people, with fixed choices or a scale, and it answers how many. Neither can show what people do, which is what observation is for, and the lessons that follow come to it.

The reason to prefer past events is the **say-do gap**: what people report about their behaviour often differs from what they do, because they forget, tidy the story and say what they think is expected. People are also poor at designing solutions, so a question such as "Which features do you want?" returns guesses. A question such as "Tell me about the last time you tried to find a setting" returns an event, and the designer can draw the conclusions.
An interviewer asks, "Don't you agree the new menu is easier to use?" and the participant says yes.

reveal.text: The wording supplied the answer. A neutral version, such as "How would you describe finding a setting last week?", leaves the answer to the participant.

steps.headline: Wording, wanting to please and self-selection each bend the answers in one direction.

lead.text: Three sources of bias account for most bad survey results. The first is wording: a **leading question** suggests the answer the asker wants, and a scale whose labels run only from "good" to "excellent" has the same effect. The second is **social desirability**, the tendency to answer as one thinks one should, which is why a question about a worthy habit overstates it. The third is **self-selection**, which arises when the people who answer are the ones who chose to, as with a pop-up that only the most annoyed or most pleased click.

These errors differ from chance error in a way that matters for the rest of the lesson. Chance error averages out as responses accumulate, but bias pushes every response the same way, so a larger survey with a biased sample is simply a more precise wrong answer.
A survey asks employees whether they exercise regularly, and the results are more flattering than the building's gym records suggest.

reveal.text: The gap between what is said and what is done is the say-do gap, and wanting to look good in front of the asker is a major cause.

steps.headline: A survey result carries a margin of error that shrinks only as the square root of the sample.

lead.text: For a proportion p measured from n independent responses, the 95% **margin of error** is 1.96 × sqrt(p(1 − p)/n). With p = 0.5 and n = 100, the margin is 1.96 × sqrt(0.25/100) = 1.96 × 0.05 = 0.098, about 9.8 percentage points, so a result of 50% means that the true value probably lies between about 40% and 60%.

The figure shows the band for four sample sizes. Because n sits under a square root, multiplying the sample by four halves the margin, from 9.8 points at n = 100 to 4.9 at n = 400, and a further factor of four brings it to about 2.5 at n = 1,600. Precision is therefore bought at an increasing price, and it covers only chance, since the formula assumes that the respondents were chosen at random.

steps.headline: Compute the 95% margin of error for p = 0.5 at n = 100 and then at n = 400.

workedSteps.text: At n = 100, p(1 − p) is 0.25 and dividing by 100 gives 0.0025, whose square root is 0.05.
Multiply by 1.96 to find the margin.
At n = 400 the square root is 0.025. Work out the margin in percentage points, to one decimal place.

lead.text: Now change the proportion. In a survey of n = 100 only a fifth of respondents, p = 0.2, prefer a feature.

reveal.text: A proportion far from 0.5 has less spread, so the margin is smaller than at p = 0.5. The worst case is always p = 0.5.

steps.headline: The question decides the method: why needs an interview, how many needs a survey, what do they do needs observation.

lead.text: With the limits of asking in hand, a method can be chosen by the question. If the team needs to know why people struggle, an interview gives reasons and examples that a closed question would miss. If it needs to know how many people struggle, a survey gives a number with a margin, provided that the sample is not biased. If it needs to know what people actually do, it should watch them, because neither interview nor survey avoids the say-do gap.

Most research questions need more than one. A common order is to interview a few people to find out what matters, to survey many to measure it, and to observe a few to check that what people say agrees with what they do.
A survey of 100 people gives a margin of 9.8 points, which is too wide. The team wants half that margin, about 4.9 points.

reveal.text: The cost grows with the square of the improvement. Four times the people halves the margin, which is why surveys are rarely sized for very small margins.

lessons.orientation: Choosing between interviews and surveys, writing a question that does not lead, and reading a margin of error.

blocks.text: A team can ask two questions about a new search feature. One is "How much do you like the new search?" and the other is "How did you find the last thing you looked for?" The first assumes that the person likes it and asks only for the amount, and it will return a number that looks like evidence. The second asks about something that happened, and its answers will include the failures.
The difference shows that asking people is a technique with failure modes of its own, and that the words of a question can decide the result before anyone answers.

blocks.text: You saw that a question's wording can supply its own answer, and that bias comes from wording, from wanting to please and from self-selection. The margin of error 1.96 × sqrt(p(1 − p)/n) fell from 9.8 to 4.9 points when n rose from 100 to 400, which means that halving it costs four times the sample, and it still covers chance only.

lead.text: A menu offers 12 choices at the first level. Each choice opens a new set of 12, and each of those opens a final set of 12 items. Work out how many items the menu can reach.

reveal.text: 1,728 items. The structure is explained in the later screens; first, how people expect content to be grouped.

steps.headline: A card sort shows how people group content, and gives ideas for a structure.

lead.text: Designers describe the organisation of a site as information architecture, and Peter Morville and Louis Rosenfeld's book of 1998 divided it into four systems: organisation, labelling, navigation and search. The first is where the company's categories and the shoppers' categories can disagree, as the figure shows for six products.

In a **card sort**, participants group cards, each naming a content item, into piles that make sense to them. In an **open card sort** they name the piles themselves, which generates ideas about structure and vocabulary. In a **closed card sort** the categories are given, and participants place the cards in them, which checks whether items fit categories that have already been chosen.

afterFigure.text: A card sort generates ideas. It does not test a navigation, because nothing is being searched for: the participants are free to sort, and the result still has to be turned into a structure and then checked by another method.

steps.headline: A tree test shows whether people can find items in a proposed structure.

lead.text: Once a structure has been proposed, a **tree test** checks it. Participants see only a text hierarchy, with no page design, search or visual cues, and are given tasks such as "Find where to change your delivery address". They click down the tree until they decide they have found the answer, and the software records where each person ended up.

Two numbers summarise the result. The **success rate** is the share of participants who ended at the correct place, and **directness** is the share who went straight there without backing up. A high success rate with low directness means that people got there by wandering, and the structure or its labels are costing them effort.

afterFigure.text: Because the design is stripped away, a failure in a tree test points at the structure or the labels, and not at a button or a layout, which tells the team where to repair.

steps.headline: Read the results of a tree test in which 20 of 25 participants reached the right leaf.

workedSteps.text: The success rate is the participants who reached the leaf divided by those who tried.
A second task has 24 participants, and 18 of them reach the right leaf. Work out its success rate as a percentage.
Compare the two tasks. The second is the one to look at first, because fewer people found the item.

lead.text: In a tree test with 25 participants, 20 reached the right leaf, and 15 of the 25 went straight to it without backing up.

reveal.text: The success rate is 80% and directness is 60%, so one participant in five failed and a further five found it only after wandering.

steps.headline: A hierarchy with b choices over d levels reaches b to the power d items.

lead.text: The shape of a structure fixes how many items it can hold. If every level offers b choices and there are d levels, then the number of items reachable is b^d, since each choice opens another set of b. In the figure, four choices at each of three levels reach 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 items, and eight choices reach 8 × 8 × 8 = 512. Twelve per level over three levels reach 1,728.

A designer can therefore trade breadth for depth. A wide menu has few levels and many choices to read on each screen, and a deep menu has few choices on each screen and more steps to take. Neither is always better: because b^d grows quickly, a short hierarchy with clear labels reaches a large catalogue, and a deep menu with clear labels can beat a wide one with vague labels.

steps.headline: Labels should use the words people use, since a structure is only as good as its names.

lead.text: A structure is read through its labels, so a hierarchy that groups correctly can still fail if its names are ones the users do not use. Internal words are the commonest cause: a company calls a section "Fulfilment" and the customer looks for "Delivery", or a bank's "Remittance" is a customer's "Send money". Card sorts give the users' words, and tree tests show where a label sent people astray.

A good label also tells people what is behind it before they click. Two labels that overlap, such as "Products" and "Solutions", send some people to the wrong branch, and show up in a tree test as a task with a low success rate and a few popular wrong answers.
A shop has about 1,000 items and wants 12 options on each screen. Work out the smallest number of levels that reaches all of them.

reveal.text: Two levels fall short at 144, and three give 1,728, so three levels suffice and a fourth would only add steps.

blocks.text: A shop's stock system files a kettle, a toaster and a lamp as small appliances, a duvet and a towel as soft goods, and a mug as ceramics, because that is how the goods are bought and stored. A shopper looking for a mug on the shop's website will go to the kitchen, and a shopper looking for a lamp will look in the bedroom. The company's categories are accurate and still useless to the person who has to find something.

Methods exist to find out how people expect content to be organised, and to check whether a structure works once it has been proposed. They are cheap to run, and they decide a design that is costly to change later, since the navigation of a site is part of every page.

recap.keyIdea: An open card sort generates a structure from people's own groupings, a tree test checks a proposed one with success rate and directness, and a hierarchy of b choices over d levels reaches b^d items.

The reach of a menu is b^d, so 12 choices over three levels reach 1,728 items. Labels in the users' own words are part of the structure.

lessons.title: Watching people use it

lead.text: A team is testing its checkout and has four possible task cards. Decide which one is best written before reading on.

reveal.text: The scenario with a goal and a deadline. The next screen explains why a task should not name the controls.

steps.headline: A usability test sets a realistic task and watches while the participant thinks aloud.

lead.text: In a moderated **usability test**, a participant works through tasks on the interface while a facilitator observes. The **think-aloud protocol** asks the participant to say what they are looking at, expecting and deciding as they go, which exposes the expectations that clicks alone would hide: a person who says "I would expect Delivery under Orders" has told the team what label and what place would have worked.

The task has to be a scenario, which gives a goal in the user's own terms, such as "Your parcel is arriving on a day you will be away; get it delivered a day later." A task that names the interface, such as "Click Orders and change the date", tests whether people can follow instructions and not whether they can find the way. The facilitator's role is to observe, and not to help or defend the design, and to probe afterwards by asking about what was seen.

afterFigure.text: Four measures come out of a test: whether the participant succeeded, how long it took, how many errors were made and how satisfied the participant felt. Success and the observed problems matter most, and satisfaction is usually collected with a questionnaire, which this lesson returns to.

lead.text: A participant says out loud, "I am looking for a way to change the date, so I am going to try the orders page." The facilitator writes it down and says nothing.

reveal.text: The participant is narrating thoughts as they work, which gives the team their expectations at the moment they matter.

steps.headline: Each user finds a share of the problems, so the first few find the most.

lead.text: Suppose each test user finds a proportion L of a product's problems, and that users find them independently. The chance that one particular problem is missed by a single user is 1 − L, the chance that n users all miss it is (1 − L)^n, and the share found is 1 − (1 − L)^n. This is the **problem discovery model** of Nielsen and Landauer.

The figure shows it with L = 0.31, where the first user finds 31%, five users find about 84% and eight find about 95%. Each added user gives less than the one before, because by then many of the problems have already been seen. The second view sets L at 0.15 for problems that are harder to stumble on, and shows that five users then find only about 56%.

afterFigure.text: Nielsen's article reports that five users find about 85% of the problems, and the exact value of the formula is 84%. The figure of L = 0.31 is an average, and it depends on the product and the tasks, so the formula is a planning guide and not a guarantee.

steps.headline: The System Usability Scale turns ten questionnaire answers into a score from 0 to 100.

lead.text: After the tasks, a participant can fill in the **System Usability Scale**, which John Brooke published in 1996. It has ten statements, such as "I think that I would like to use this system frequently" and "I found the system unnecessarily complex", each answered from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The statements alternate between positive and negative, so the scoring differs for odd and even items.

For an odd item, the contribution is the response minus 1, and for an even item it is 5 minus the response, which puts every item on a scale of 0 to 4 with 4 the best. The ten contributions are added and the sum is multiplied by 2.5, giving a score from 0 to 100. In the figure, a participant who answered 4 on every odd item and 2 on every even item gets 3 from each item, a sum of 30, and a score of 75.

afterFigure.text: The score is not a percentage and not a share of anything. It is a position on a 0 to 100 scale, and the figure of about 68 is the commonly quoted average from many studies, so a score is read against that and against the same product's earlier score.

steps.headline: Test in small rounds, fix what is found, and test again.

lead.text: The claim behind five users is that five per round find most of the problems for one group of users, and not that five is a whole study. The usual plan is to test with a few people, fix the problems found, and test again, because fixing the obvious ones lets the next round reach the less obvious ones, and because a different group of users, such as novices and experts, has different problems and needs its own round.

A test can be moderated, with a facilitator present, or unmoderated, run by software without one, and it can be in person or remote. Moderated tests allow probing and are best for finding why. Unmoderated tests are cheaper and reach many people, and they suit measuring success and time on clear tasks.
A team wants to find at least 90% of the problems in one round, with L = 0.31. Work out the smallest number of users that achieves this.

reveal.text: The gain per user falls quickly, so moving from 84% to 90% takes two more users and getting to 99% takes many more.

lessons.orientation: Think-aloud tests, the discovery formula and the SUS score.
lessons.nextAction: Compare two designs in an experiment, and decide whether a difference in the numbers is real.

blocks.text: Jakob Nielsen and Thomas Landauer reported in 1993 that if each test user finds a proportion L of a product's usability problems, then n users find 1 − (1 − L)^n of them, and that L averaged about 0.31 across the projects they studied. With L = 0.31 and n = 5 the formula gives 1 − 0.69^5 = 0.8436, which is the origin of the widely repeated advice that five users are enough.

The advice is more careful than its slogan, and the arithmetic shows why: the first few users find many problems and later users find fewer new ones, so a small test repeated after fixes beats a large one that is run once. A test like that can be run, something measured, and ten questionnaire answers turned into a score.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a task for a usability test, compute the share of problems a number of users finds, and score a SUS sheet.
intro.whyItMatters: A small test run repeatedly finds more than a large test run once.

recap.keyIdea: A think-aloud test with scenario tasks reveals problems, n users find 1 − (1 − L)^n of them, so tests are run in small rounds, and ten SUS answers become a 0 to 100 score.

blocks.text: You wrote a task as a goal and not as instructions, and saw that with L = 0.31 five users find about 84% of the problems while the gain from each extra user shrinks. A SUS sheet is scored by taking response − 1 for odd items and 5 − response for even ones, summing and multiplying by 2.5, and the result is read against an average near 68.

lessons.title: Experiments and analytics

lead.text: A has 4.0% conversion and B has 4.8%, with 1,000 visitors in each group. Decide how far the data support shipping B.

reveal.text: The difference is not established by this test. The rest of the lesson shows how to check.

steps.headline: An A/B test assigns users to versions at random, so a difference can be put down to the version.

lead.text: In an **A/B test**, each visitor is assigned by chance to version A or version B, and a metric such as the share who sign up is compared. Random assignment is what makes the comparison fair, since it spreads every other difference between users, such as new against returning visitors or mobile against desktop, evenly across the two groups. Without it, B might simply have been shown to the more enthusiastic users.

The metric is a proportion, and it varies from one group of users to the next even if the versions are identical, in the way a coin tossed a thousand times does not give exactly 500 heads. The question for the analysis is therefore how large the observed gap is compared with that natural variation.
A site shows version B to everyone who visits on a Monday and version A on all other days.

reveal.text: That is not random assignment, since Monday visitors may differ from other visitors. Assigning each visitor by chance removes that problem.

steps.headline: The z statistic divides the observed difference by the variation that chance alone would give.

lead.text: For two conversion rates p1 and p2 from n1 and n2 users, the variation of the difference is its standard error, sqrt(p1(1 − p1)/n1 + p2(1 − p2)/n2), and the statistic is **z** = (p2 − p1) divided by that standard error. A large z means the observed difference is large compared with the chance variation, and at the 95% level a difference is called significant when |z| exceeds 1.96.

For the opening example, with p1 = 0.040, p2 = 0.048 and n = 1,000 each, the standard error is sqrt(0.0000384 + 0.0000457) = sqrt(0.0000841), about 0.00917, so z = 0.008/0.00917, about 0.87. The figure draws the two rates as bell curves that show how much each could vary: at 1,000 users each they overlap heavily, and with ten times the users the curves narrow and the same difference gives z = 2.76.

afterFigure.text: The calculation uses the same difference throughout, and only the sample size changes, which is why a small test can miss a real difference and a very large one can find a trivial one.

diagram.caption: The curves show how much each measured rate could vary by chance. More users make them narrower, so the same difference separates them.

steps.headline: Work out z for 4.0% against 4.8% with 1,000 users in each group.

workedSteps.text: Each rate has a variance p(1 − p)/n, and the two are added to give the variance of the difference.
The standard error is the square root of that sum.
Divide the difference of 0.008 by the standard error, to two decimal places.

lead.text: Try a larger difference. The observed difference is 0.03 and its standard error is 0.012.

reveal.text: The ratio exceeds 1.96, so this difference is significant, and it would be unlikely to arise by chance alone.

steps.headline: Significance means chance rarely produces a difference this large, and it says nothing about its size or cause.

lead.text: A result with |z| above 1.96 is called **statistically significant** at the 95% level. It means that if the two versions were really the same, a difference this large would arise by chance less than one time in twenty. It does not prove that B is better by any amount, and it does not say that the difference matters, since a very large test can find a gain too small to be worth shipping.

The reverse also needs care. A result below 1.96, as in the opening example, does not show that the versions are equal. It shows that the test could not tell them apart, and a larger sample might still find a difference.
A test gives z = 2.3. Use the 95% rule to say how the difference should be described.

reveal.text: A z of 2.3 exceeds 1.96, so the difference is statistically significant, and the size of the gain still has to be judged on its own.

steps.headline: Fix the sample size in advance, since stopping when the result looks good inflates false positives.

lead.text: The 95% rule assumes that the analysis is run once, on a sample size decided before the test began. A team that looks at the result each morning and stops at the first day on which |z| exceeds 1.96 gives chance many more chances to cross the line, and the share of false wins rises well above one in twenty. The remedy is to decide how many users to test, from the smallest difference worth detecting, and to read the result only when that number has been reached.

Analytics have a second limit, which is that they record what users did and not why. The funnel in the figure shows 1,000 users at step 1, 800 at step 2, 800 at step 3 and 320 who finish, so 480 of the 800 who reach step 3 leave, which is 60%. The counts locate the problem exactly and are silent about its cause, which is the **why gap**, and it is closed by watching or asking the people who left.

afterFigure.text: Two methods therefore work together. Analytics and A/B tests say what happened and how much, and the think-aloud tests and interviews of the previous lessons say why.

blocks.text: A team tests two versions of a sign-up page. Version A converts 4.0% of visitors and version B converts 4.8%, from 1,000 visitors each, so B looks 20% better. The team is ready to ship B, and the numbers show that it should hesitate: with groups of this size, two identical versions would often differ by that much.

An experiment gives a definite answer only when the difference is larger than chance can easily produce, and the test for that is a short calculation. Even then it says what happened and not why, so the two methods, the A/B test and the qualitative follow-up, answer different questions.

recap.keyIdea: An A/B test assigns users at random, a difference is distinguishable from chance when |z| exceeds 1.96, the sample size must be fixed in advance, and analytics show what users did and not why.

blocks.text: You saw that 4.0% against 4.8% with 1,000 users each gives z = 0.87, which chance can easily produce, and that the same gap with ten times the users gives z = 2.76. A result is read against 1.96, the sample size is set before the test, and a funnel of counts still needs interviews or tests to explain it.

lessons.title: Ten usability heuristics

lead.text: Picture a file upload that runs for twenty seconds. The screen shows a spinner, and nothing else, for the whole time. Decide which kind of information the user is missing.

reveal.text: The user is missing information about what the system is doing. The first heuristic is about exactly that.

steps.headline: The ten heuristics are rules of thumb that prompt questions about a design.

lead.text: A **usability heuristic** is a broad rule of thumb, not a precise rule: it says what a good interface tends to do and leaves the evaluator to decide whether a given screen does it. Nielsen's list has ten, and the figure gives their names in order. They are guides to what to look for, and they do not settle disputes, since a design can satisfy one by breaking another.

Because the rules are broad, a single problem can break more than one of them. A message that reads "Error 0x80070057" breaks the rule about plain language and the rule about explaining errors, and the evaluator should record the one that explains the most. The rest of the lesson goes through the ten in turn, and the later lesson on inspection shows how to apply them systematically.

steps.headline: The first three heuristics concern what the user is told, how it is said, and the way out.

lead.text: **Visibility of system status** asks the system to keep users informed about what is going on, with feedback in reasonable time. A twenty-second upload with no progress indicator breaks it. **Match between system and the real world** asks the system to speak the user's language, with words and concepts the user knows and not internal terms, and to follow real-world conventions. An error code such as 0x80070057 is the opposite of that.

**User control and freedom** acknowledges that users often choose an action by mistake and need a clearly marked emergency exit, such as undo, cancel and back. A record that is deleted immediately, with no way back, breaks it. The figure shows all three: a silent spinner, an error code and an immediate delete.

reveal.text: The user has no way out of an action they may not have meant, and the heuristic that names that need is control and freedom.

steps.headline: Four more heuristics cover sameness, prevention, memory and speed.

lead.text: **Consistency and standards** says that users should not have to wonder whether different words, situations or actions mean the same thing, and that conventions of the platform and of other products should be followed. **Error prevention** goes further than a good error message, since it removes the conditions in which an error is likely, or asks for confirmation before a costly action. **Recognition rather than recall**, met in the lesson on memory, asks that objects, actions and options be visible, so that users need not remember information from one part of the interface to another.

**Flexibility and efficiency of use** says that accelerators, unseen by the novice, may speed the interaction for the expert, such as keyboard shortcuts and the ability to tailor frequent actions. The same screen then serves both groups.
A site shows its main button in blue with the label Save on one page and in grey with the label Submit on another.

reveal.text: The same action appears under two names and two styles. The heuristic about sameness is consistency and standards.

lead.text: A checkout asks the user to type a long product code that was printed on a page that is no longer on screen.

reveal.text: The code has to be carried in memory from one page to the next, which the lesson on working memory showed is costly. The heuristic is recognition rather than recall.

steps.headline: The last three concern what to leave out, how to explain errors, and where help lives.

lead.text: **Aesthetic and minimalist design** says that screens should not contain information that is irrelevant or rarely needed, since every extra unit of information competes with the relevant units and lowers their visibility. **Help users recognize, diagnose and recover from errors** says that error messages should be expressed in plain language, with no codes, say precisely what went wrong and suggest a solution. **Help and documentation** accepts that the best system needs no explanation, but says that where help is needed, it should be easy to search, focused on the user's task and short.

A short rule resolves overlaps. When a problem fits several heuristics, name the one that explains it best and say how it connects to the others. The code 0x80070057 is most fully explained by the error heuristic, since it describes what the message must contain, while its failure to speak the user's language is a secondary cause.

steps.headline: Assign 'Error 0x80070057' to the heuristic that explains it best.

workedSteps.text: The message gives only a code, which is not in the user's language, so match between system and the real world applies.
It also gives no cause and no step the user can take, which a second heuristic covers more fully, because it says what an error message must contain.
Name the heuristic that requires a plain statement of the problem and a suggested fix.

lead.text: A settings page shows forty options with equal weight, and the option a user needs is lost among rarely used ones.

reveal.text: Each extra option competes with the ones that matter. The heuristic about leaving out the unneeded is aesthetic and minimalist design.

blocks.text: Jakob Nielsen and Rolf Molich presented heuristic evaluation in 1990, and in 1994 Nielsen refined the list into the ten heuristics still used today, after analysing a large set of real usability problems to see which broad rules explained the most of them. The rules are short enough to remember and general enough to apply to a web page, an aircraft display or a kitchen appliance.

A heuristic is a broad rule of thumb for judging an interface, and the usefulness of the list is that it gives names to the problems that evaluators keep meeting. A reviewer who sees a spinner that runs for twenty seconds with no message can say which rule it breaks, and the name suggests the repair.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name Nielsen's ten heuristics and assign a described problem to the one it breaks.
intro.whyItMatters: Names for common problems let a team talk about them and point to a repair.

recap.keyIdea: Nielsen's ten heuristics are rules of thumb that name common usability problems, and a problem is assigned to the heuristic that explains it best.

blocks.text: You went through the ten in three groups: status, plain language and control; consistency, error prevention, recognition and efficiency; and minimalism, error messages and help. A single problem can break several of them, so the evaluator names the one that explains the most and notes the others.

lessons.title: Inspecting an interface and rating what you find

lead.text: Each of two evaluators independently finds 35% of an interface's problems. Estimate what share they find together; the answer is not 70%.

reveal.text: About 57.8%, because the two overlap. The next screens give the method behind the number.

steps.headline: In a heuristic evaluation, several evaluators inspect alone, then merge what they found.

lead.text: Inspection differs from testing in that no users take part. In a **heuristic evaluation**, a small group of evaluators each go through the interface on their own, comparing it with the heuristics from the previous lesson and noting each problem with the screen it is on and the heuristic it breaks. Only afterwards do they meet to merge their lists into one.

The independent first pass is the heart of the method. If the evaluators agreed beforehand, or looked at one another's notes, they would tend to find the same things, and the lists would overlap more than they need to. Working alone, each person's quirks and experience turn up a different part of the problems, and the merge collects them.

afterFigure.text: Inspection does not replace testing. It finds different problems, since experts miss some that real users hit and report others that no user would care about, so the two methods are used together.

lead.text: Three evaluators agree on a review plan together, and then inspect the interface as one group, discussing as they go.

reveal.text: That removes the independence the method depends on. The evaluators should each inspect alone first, so that their findings differ.

steps.headline: Each evaluator finds only part of the problems, and the finds combine more slowly than they add.

lead.text: If one evaluator finds 35% of the problems, the chance that a given problem is missed by that evaluator is 0.65. If evaluators work independently, the chance that n of them all miss it is 0.65^n, and the share found is 1 − 0.65^n. For two evaluators this is about 57.8%, for three about 72.5%, and for five about 88.4%, as the figure shows. The second view of the figure follows the three-evaluator case.

The increase from each extra evaluator shrinks, from 22.8 points for the second to 14.7 for the third and 9.6 for the fourth, which is why most teams use three to five evaluators and not twenty. The figures assume independence, and real evaluators overlap more than that, so they are best taken as optimistic.

The share found is what remains.
Now a fourth evaluator joins. Work out the share found by four, to one decimal place.

steps.headline: Each problem gets a rating from 0 to 4, based on how often, how badly and how persistently it bites.

lead.text: Not every problem deserves the same effort, so each is given a **severity rating**. Nielsen's scale runs from 0 to 4: 0 means the evaluator does not agree that it is a usability problem, 1 is cosmetic and to be fixed if time allows, 2 is minor, 3 is major and important to fix, and 4 is a usability catastrophe that must be fixed before release.

Three factors decide the rating. **Frequency** asks how many users meet the problem, **impact** asks how hard it is for them to overcome, and **persistence** asks whether they will be caught by it every time or learn to avoid it. A mislabelled button that every user meets on every visit and cannot avoid rates higher than a typo on a settings page that few see. The figure shows a findings log before and after rating, with a hidden Pay button at 4 and a typo at 1.

steps.headline: A cognitive walkthrough steps through a task and asks four questions at every action.

lead.text: The **cognitive walkthrough**, described by Wharton, Rieman, Lewis and Polson in 1994, inspects an interface for how easily a new user can learn it. The evaluator takes a task, lists the actions that the interface requires, and at each action asks four questions. Will the user try to achieve the right effect? Will the user notice that the correct action is available? Will the user connect the correct action with the effect they want? If the action is taken, will the user see that progress is being made towards the goal?

A heuristic evaluation looks at a whole screen and asks which rules it breaks, whereas a walkthrough looks at one task path and asks where a first-time user would go wrong. The four questions correspond to the gulfs of the earlier lesson: the first three concern execution, and the fourth concerns evaluation.
Look again at the walkthrough. At every action in the task, the evaluator asks the same set of questions.

reveal.text: Try, notice, connect and see progress make four. The first three are about acting, and the last is about reading the result.

steps.headline: Choose an inspection method by what you have and what you need to know.

lead.text: The methods of the last few lessons suit different situations. A heuristic evaluation needs evaluators and an interface or a mock-up, and no users, so it fits a week with no participants. A cognitive walkthrough fits a design for first-time users, such as a sign-up flow. A usability test or a tree test needs participants and finds what real people do, which no inspection can promise.

Whatever the method, the output is a list of problems with severities, and the severities set the order of the work. A team with three evaluators and one test has a sound plan: the inspection finds the cheap problems before the test, so that the test time is spent on the ones that only users reveal.
Suppose the evaluators are less experienced, and each finds only 20% of the problems, independently. Work out the smallest number of them who find at least 75% together.

reveal.text: Weaker evaluators cost more people for the same coverage, which is a reason to use experienced evaluators and to supplement the review with a test.

lessons.nextAction: Write error messages and forms that prevent mistakes and help people recover from the ones that happen.

blocks.text: A single evaluator who inspects an interface against the heuristics finds only part of its problems. In studies that Nielsen reports, the share is around a third, and if each of three evaluators works alone and finds 35%, then the chance that a particular problem escapes all three is 0.65 × 0.65 × 0.65 = 0.2746, so together they find about 72.5% of the problems. The figure for one evaluator is a poor guide to what a team of three will do.

Such an evaluation is organised in a particular way, the problems it finds can be ranked by how much they matter, and a second inspection method, the cognitive walkthrough, asks a different set of questions about the same interface.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to estimate what a group of evaluators finds, rate a problem on the 0 to 4 scale, and choose between a heuristic evaluation and a walkthrough.
intro.whyItMatters: Inspection is quick and cheap, and severity tells a team what to fix first.

recap.keyIdea: Evaluators inspect alone and merge their findings, a group of n finds 1 − (1 − L)^n of the problems, severity from 0 to 4 sets the order of repair, and a walkthrough asks four questions at each action of a task.

blocks.text: You worked out that two evaluators who each find 35% together find 57.8% and three find 72.5%, and that the gain from each addition shrinks. Severity combines frequency, impact and persistence into a rating from 0 to 4, and a cognitive walkthrough looks at one task path with four questions at each action. Inspection finds problems before a test, and does not replace one.
