lessons.title: Forms, errors and feedback

lead.text: A date field offers a calendar picker that shows only real dates. Decide what that does to the error of typing a date such as 31 February.

reveal.text: It makes the error impossible. The next screen sets out the ways of preventing errors.

steps.headline: The best error message is the one that never needs to appear.

lead.text: Psychologists distinguish two kinds of error, and both occur in forms. In a **slip** the user has the right goal and performs the wrong action, as when a finger hits the wrong key, and in a **mistake** the goal or the plan is wrong, as when the user has misunderstood what a field asks for. Slips are the more common, and design can reduce both.

Prevention comes first, because it removes the error and does not have to describe it. A **constraint** limits the options to valid ones, as a calendar picker does for dates and a numeric keypad does for a phone number. A **default** supplies a sensible value so that most users do not have to type or choose anything, and **formatting help**, such as an example beside a field or automatic spacing in a card number, lets the user see the expected shape before making an error. Each of these is an application of Nielsen's heuristic on error prevention.
Look at the plug and the picker again: each limits the user to valid choices, and neither needs a message.

reveal.text: The general name is a constraint. It is the strongest form of prevention, because the wrong action is simply not available.

steps.headline: A good error message says what happened, why, and what to do next, beside the field.

lead.text: Some errors cannot be prevented, and then the message has to carry the whole repair. A good message has three parts: it says **what happened**, it says **why**, and it says **what to do next**, in the user's words and not the system's, so "The email address is missing an @. Enter it like name@example.com." in place of "Invalid input." It sits next to the field it concerns, and the field is also marked in a way that does not rely on colour alone.

The figure shows a failed submit three ways. With no message, the user has to find the problem unaided, and with a general message at the top of the page they must read it, then look for the field, and then work out what is wrong. With a message beside the field, the three parts are in the place where the user is already looking.

afterFigure.text: The message should also be polite and should not blame the user, since the aim is to get the form completed. It is also where accessibility begins: success criterion 3.3.1, Error Identification, in WCAG 2.2, requires that an error in an input be identified and described to the user in text.

workedSteps.text: Count the parts of a good message that 'Invalid input.' supplies. It names no field, gives no cause and offers no fix.
Add what happened and why, in the user's words: 'The email address is missing an @.'
Add what to do next, with an example of a valid value: 'Enter it like name@example.com.'
Place the message directly under the Email field, and mark the field itself as well as the text.

lead.text: A shop's card field has received a number with one digit missing. Choose the message that follows the three-part rule.

reveal.text: The good message names the field, gives the rule and the user's count, and so lets the user act without guessing.

steps.headline: Letting a user reverse an action works better than asking them to confirm it.

lead.text: A confirmation dialog, "Are you sure?", looks like protection, and it works poorly for actions that are meant. Users who see the dialog on every deletion answer it by habit, and the one time it matters they click through it. A reversible action with an **undo**, as Gmail offers for a few seconds after sending a message, costs nothing when the action was intended and rescues the user when it was not.

Confirmation still has a place for actions that cannot be reversed, such as permanently deleting an account, and then the dialog should say exactly what will be lost, with a button named for the action and not "OK". Elsewhere, undo is the better design, and it applies the heuristic of user control and freedom.
A mail app lets a sender take back a message for ten seconds after pressing Send, with no dialog beforehand.

reveal.text: Reversal after the action, and no dialog before it, is the pattern that works for reversible actions.

steps.headline: Labels, types and attributes in the markup carry the form's meaning to browsers and screen readers.

lead.text: A form's behaviour rests on its markup. A visible **label** element, tied to its field by the for and id attributes, gives the field a name that stays on screen and is announced by a screen reader, and clicking it moves focus to the field. An **in-field hint** is text inside the field that disappears when typing begins, so it is not a replacement for a label.

The **type** attribute lets the browser check the shape of a value, so type="email" asks for something that looks like an address, and **required** makes the browser reject an empty field. **autocomplete** says what the field is for, so that the browser can fill it in, which helps people who find typing slow or difficult, and WCAG 2.2 also asks, in criterion 3.3.7, that a form not make users enter the same information twice in one process.

afterFigure.text: Validation can run when the user leaves a field, which is inline validation and avoids a wall of errors at the end, but it should not fire while the user is still typing an address that is not yet complete.

lessons.title: WCAG and contrast

lead.text: Accessibility work is often described as being for a small group. Decide which description of the people who benefit is most accurate.

reveal.text: Limits can be permanent, temporary or situational, and each group is larger than people expect. The next screen starts with how WCAG organises its requirements.

steps.headline: WCAG groups its requirements under four principles and three levels.

lead.text: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines are published by the World Wide Web Consortium. Version 2.0 appeared in 2008, 2.1 in 2018 and 2.2 in October 2023, each building on the one before, and 2.2 dropped the old criterion 4.1.1 on parsing, because it had become obsolete. Every requirement is a **success criterion** with a number, and the criteria sit under four principles, which spell **POUR**: content must be **Perceivable**, so that users can sense it, **Operable**, so that they can work it, **Understandable**, so that they can follow it, and **Robust**, so that different browsers and assistive technologies can interpret it.

Each criterion also has a level. **Level A** is the basic requirement, **AA** adds the requirements that most laws and policies call for, and **AAA** is the strictest, and rarely required in full for a whole site. When a policy says that a site must conform to WCAG 2.2, it usually means all the A and AA criteria.

lead.text: Criterion 2.1.1 requires that everything that can be done with a mouse can also be done from a keyboard.

reveal.text: That concerns the controls, and the principle that covers whether controls can be worked is Operable.

steps.headline: The contrast ratio compares the lighter and darker colours through their relative luminance.

lead.text: Every colour has a **relative luminance** L, a number from 0 for black to 1 for white that estimates how much light it gives out as the eye perceives it. The **contrast ratio** of two colours is (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05), where L1 is the lighter colour's luminance and L2 the darker's. The 0.05 stands for the light that always reaches the eye from the surroundings. Black on white gives (1 + 0.05) / (0 + 0.05) = 21, the largest value possible, and two identical colours give 1.

To find L for a colour from its red, green and blue values, each channel is divided by 255 and then linearised, and the results are combined as L = 0.2126 R + 0.7152 G + 0.0722 B. For #767676 each channel is 118 out of 255, which linearises to about 0.181, so L is 0.181 and the ratio against white is 1.05 / 0.231, about 4.54. The figure places four pairs on the scale.

afterFigure.text: The weights differ because the eye is most sensitive to green and least to blue, so a pure blue on white gives a ratio of about 8.6 while a pure green is lighter and gives much less.

steps.headline: Compute the contrast ratio for L1 = 0.5 and L2 = 0.05, then for L1 = 0.8 and L2 = 0.2.

workedSteps.text: Add 0.05 to each luminance, so that the numerator is 0.55 and the denominator is 0.10.
Divide the numerator by the denominator.
The ratio of 5.5 is above 4.5, so the pair passes AA for normal text.
Now take L1 = 0.8 and L2 = 0.2. Work out the ratio, to one decimal place.

lead.text: Use the formula on the two extreme colours, with L = 1 for white and L = 0 for black.

reveal.text: The result is the top of the scale, and it shows why any real pair of colours falls between 1 and this value.

steps.headline: AA needs 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text and key interface parts.

lead.text: Under criterion 1.4.3, Contrast (Minimum), text must have a ratio of at least 4.5 to 1, except that **large text**, which is 18 point or larger, or 14 point bold or larger, needs only 3 to 1, because bigger letters are easier to read. Under criterion 1.4.11, Non-text Contrast, the parts of controls that a user needs to see, such as the border of a text field, and the key parts of graphics need at least 3 to 1 against their surroundings. Level AAA asks for 7 to 1 for normal text.

The tests are exact. WCAG says that the computed values should not be rounded, so a ratio of 4.499 fails and the pair #777777 on white, at 4.48, fails by a hair. A designer who checks a colour with a tool is therefore doing the comparison that the criterion states, and a grey that merely looks readable proves nothing.
Large text, at 18 point or larger, has a lower requirement than normal text at level AA, which is 4.5 to 1.

reveal.text: The lower figure is the same one that applies to the parts of controls under 1.4.11.

steps.headline: Colour must not be the only way to carry a meaning.

lead.text: Contrast is not the only way in which colour can fail a reader. Criterion 1.4.1, Use of Color, says that colour must not be the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action or distinguishing an element. A link that differs from the text around it only by hue is invisible to a reader who cannot tell the two hues apart, and an error shown only as red text cannot be seen by them either.

The repair is to add a second cue that does not depend on colour, such as an underline for links and a mark or a word for errors. The figure shows the same sentence with colour alone and with an underline added. Contrast and colour use are both about whether people can perceive what is on the screen, and both fall under Perceivable.

blocks.text: The text colour #767676 on a white background gives a contrast ratio of 4.54 to 1, and the colour #777777, one step lighter in each channel, gives 4.48 to 1. The two greys look the same to almost everyone, and yet the first meets the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines at level AA for normal text and the second does not, because the line is drawn at 4.5 and WCAG says that computed values must not be rounded.

That precision is possible because the guidelines turn a vague wish, text that can be read, into numbers that can be checked. The guidelines are organised in a particular way, and a contrast ratio can be computed from two colours, so that a designer can check a pair before a user has to struggle with it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to name the four WCAG principles, compute a contrast ratio from two luminance values, and judge whether a colour pair meets AA.
intro.whyItMatters: Contrast turns readable into a number a designer can check in seconds.

recap.keyIdea: WCAG 2.2 groups its criteria under Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust, at levels A, AA and AAA, and AA needs a contrast ratio of 4.5 to 1 for normal text and 3 to 1 for large text and key interface parts.

blocks.text: You computed contrast ratios from two relative luminances, found that black on white gives 21 and that 4.48 fails where 4.54 passes, and saw that the ratio is never rounded. A meaning carried by colour alone fails readers who cannot see the difference, so a second cue is added.

A page contains these five elements in one row: Home
Menu
Next Decide how many of them a keyboard user can reach by pressing Tab.

steps.headline: Every function must work from the keyboard, and the user must be able to see where focus is.

lead.text: WCAG success criterion 2.1.1 requires that all functionality be operable through a keyboard interface, and that is level A. The Tab key moves **focus** from one interactive element to the next, and Enter or Space activates it. Native links, buttons and form fields are in the Tab order by default. A div or a span with an onclick handler is not, and ignores Enter and Space as well, so it works for a mouse user and for no one else.

Two further criteria concern focus itself. Criterion 2.4.7, Focus Visible, requires a visible indicator of where focus is, which is why removing the outline with CSS and supplying nothing in its place is a failure. Criterion 2.4.11, Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), which is new in WCAG 2.2, requires that the focused element is not entirely hidden behind other content such as a sticky header or a cookie banner. The figure shows the same row of controls built two ways.

lead.text: A developer wants a Save control that works with Tab, Enter and Space without writing any extra scripts.

reveal.text: The button element gives all three, together with its role, so a div is never needed for a control that performs an action.

steps.headline: Native elements give assistive technology a name, a role and a state with no extra code.

lead.text: A screen reader does not see the page as the eye does. It reads the markup, and for each control it announces a name, a role and a state, such as "Save, button" or "Email, edit text, required". Criterion 4.1.2, Name, Role, Value, requires these to be available to assistive technology. A native **button** supplies them automatically, and a div supplies none unless a role, a name, key handling and focus are all added by hand, which is more work and easier to get wrong.

The same principle covers the rest of the page. A **label** tied to its field gives the field its name, as the previous lesson showed. **Headings** from h1 down form an outline that screen reader users move through, so they should follow the structure of the content and not the size the designer wants. Links, which go to another page, use the a element with an href, and buttons, which do something on this page, use button.

steps.headline: Choose the element for each control on a product page.

workedSteps.text: The Add to basket control changes the basket and stays on the page, so it performs an action. The element is a button.
The Delivery information control opens a different page, so it navigates, and it should be a link with an href.
State which element a control uses when it takes the user to another page.
The field for a postcode needs a name that a screen reader can announce, which a label tied to the field provides.

steps.headline: An image needs the alt text that matches its job, and a decorative image needs none.

lead.text: Criterion 1.1.1, Non-text Content, asks for a text alternative for non-text content, and the right text depends on what the image is for. An **informative** image carries a message, so its alt text states that message, as for a chart that shows sales rising. A **functional** image is used as a control, as with a magnifier icon in a search button, and its alt text names what the control does, here Search, and not what it looks like. A **decorative** image carries nothing, and it takes an empty alt attribute, alt="", so that a screen reader skips it.

Adding descriptive text to every image is a mistake, because a decorative flourish read aloud as "wavy line" slows the user and says nothing. An image with no alt attribute at all is worse, since some screen readers then read the file name. The figure shows one image of each kind.

diagram.alt: Three kinds of image: an informative bar chart whose alt text states its message, a functional magnifier icon whose alt text is Search, and a decorative wavy divider with an empty alt.

steps.headline: Pointer targets must be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels at AA.

lead.text: Small targets are hard to hit for anyone with a tremor, a large thumb or a moving bus, and Fitts's law says why: a small W makes the index of difficulty larger. Criterion 2.5.8, Target Size (Minimum), new in WCAG 2.2 at level AA, requires that pointer targets be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels. A smaller target passes if a 24 pixel circle centred on it does not meet another target, which is the **spacing exception**. The figure shows a 20 pixel target against the 24 pixel line.

The enhanced criterion 2.5.5, at level AAA, asks for 44 by 44 CSS pixels, and it is a sound aim for important controls. Links inside a sentence are exempt from both, since their height follows the text around them.

steps.headline: Pages must still work when text is enlarged or the window is narrow.

lead.text: Two last criteria concern magnification. Criterion 1.4.4, Resize Text, requires that text can be resized to 200% without losing content or function, and 1.4.10, Reflow, requires that a page can be viewed at a width of 320 CSS pixels without scrolling in two directions. A layout of fixed-width columns fails the second, while one that stacks at narrow widths passes it, which is also what a phone needs.

A short audit therefore runs in a fixed order. Unplug the mouse and Tab through the page, then check that each control is a native element with a name, that images have the right alt, that fields have labels, that targets are at least 24 pixels, and that the page reflows at 320 pixels.
